sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/0528bbd9167b17228b702a5c4b9c3c62]

In the [MATH: xy]-plane shown, rhombus [MATH: EFGH] has its diagonals aligned along the [MATH: x]- and [MATH: y]-axes. What is the area, in square units, of the rhombus?

sections.normalized_html:
We are given that [MATH: EFGH] is a rhombus, which means all of its sides are congruent and its diagonals intersect at right angles. So, [MATH: \overline{EG}] divides this rhombus into two congruent triangles, [MATH: \triangle{EFG}] and [MATH: \triangle{EHG}.]

The formula for the area of a triangle is given by [MATH: A_t = \dfrac{b \cdot h}{2},] where [MATH: b] is the base length of the triangle and [MATH: h] is the height of the triangle.

In our case, each triangle has a base length of [MATH: b = 7 - (-7) = 14] units, while its height is [MATH: h = 5.] Therefore, the area of each triangle, in square units, is [MATH: A_{t}|= (b ⋅ h)/(2); = (14 ⋅ 5)/(2); = (70)/(2); = 35.]

Finally, since [MATH: \triangle{EFG}] and [MATH: \triangle{EHG}] are congruent, the area of each is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] of the area of rhombus [MATH: EFGH.] Therefore, the area of rhombus [MATH: EFGH,] in square units, is [MATH: A_{r}|= 2 ⋅ A_{t}; = 2 ⋅ 35; = 70.]

sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/187f9a54052b35783351bac5702aa236]

In the coordinate plane, the segment shown represents one of the legs of a right triangle. The area of this triangle is [MATH: 54\sqrt{5}] square units. What is the length, in units, of the other leg of this triangle?

sections.normalized_html:
Let's remember that if [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] have coordinates [MATH: (x_1,y_1)] and [MATH: (x_2,y_2),] respectively, the distance between [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] is given by [MATH: d(P,Q) = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}.]

We proceed to find the length [MATH: x] of the first leg of the right triangle, whose endpoints are [MATH: (1,3)] and [MATH: (4,9).] To do this, we use the formula for the distance between points given above: [MATH: x|= sqrt((4 − 1)^{2} + (9 − 3)^{2}); = sqrt(3^{2} + 6^{2}); = sqrt(9 + 36); = sqrt(45); = sqrt(9 ⋅ 5); = sqrt(9) ⋅ sqrt(5); = 3sqrt(5)]

Let [MATH: y] be the length of the second leg. We're told the area [MATH: A] of the triangle is [MATH: 54\sqrt{5}] square units. Since the area of a right triangle is found by multiplying the lengths of its two legs and then dividing that product by two, we can find [MATH: y] as follows: [MATH: A|= 54sqrt(5); (x ⋅ y)/(2)|= 54sqrt(5); (3sqrt(5) ⋅ y)/(2)|= 54sqrt(5); y|= (2 ⋅ 54sqrt(5))/(3sqrt(5)); y|= 2 ⋅ 18; y|= 36]

Therefore, the length of the second leg of the triangle is [MATH: 36] units.

items.title: Finding the Area of a Triangle

sections.normalized_html: The vertices of [MATH: \triangle ABC] have coordinates [MATH: A(1,1),] [MATH: B(2,5),] and [MATH: C(6,2).] Find the area of [MATH: \triangle ABC.]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/94eabfeb47ad89de154fcca136307106]

The vertices of [MATH: \triangle ABC] have coordinates [MATH: A(1,1),] [MATH: B(2,5),] and [MATH: C(6,2).] Find the area of [MATH: \triangle ABC.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, note that we can inscribe our triangle within the rectangle shown in the diagram below.

We have the rectangle, whose area we denote by [MATH: A,] and four triangles:

  • [MATH: \triangle ABC,] whose area [MATH: A_{\triangle}] we're required to determine,

  • the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB}] and area [MATH: A_1,]

  • the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC}] and area [MATH: A_2,] and

  • the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC}] and area [MATH: A_3.]

Recall that the area of a figure consisting of several smaller non-overlapping parts is equal to the sum of the areas of those parts. So, we have

[MATH: A = A_{\triangle} + A_1 + A_2 + A_3,] which means that

[MATH: A_{\triangle} = A - A_1 - A_2 - A_3.]

Let's now compute all the areas on the right-hand side of this equation.

  • For the area of the rectangle, we have [MATH: A|= width ⋅ height; = 5 ⋅ 4; = 20.]

  • For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB},] we have [MATH: A_{1}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 1 ⋅ 4; = 2.]

  • For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC},] we have [MATH: A_{2}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 4 ⋅ 3; = 6.]

  • For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC},] we have [MATH: A_{3}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 5 ⋅ 1; = 2.5.]

Therefore, the area of [MATH: \triangle ABC] is

[MATH: A_{\triangle} = 20 - 2 - 6 - 2.5 = 9.5]

square units.

Explanation:
First, note that we can inscribe our triangle within the rectangle shown in the diagram below.

[IMG: /graphics/71c04a9cc861d1af2da92e961efb1512]

We have the rectangle, whose area we denote by [MATH: A,] and four triangles:

- [MATH: \triangle ABC,] whose area [MATH: A_{\triangle}] we're required to determine,
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB}] and area [MATH: A_1,]
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC}] and area [MATH: A_2,] and
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC}] and area [MATH: A_3.]

Recall that the area of a figure consisting of several smaller non-overlapping parts is equal to the sum of the areas of those parts. So, we have

[MATH: A = A_{\triangle} + A_1 + A_2 + A_3,]
which means that

[MATH: A_{\triangle} = A - A_1 - A_2 - A_3.]

Let's now compute all the areas on the right-hand side of this equation.

- For the area of the rectangle, we have
[MATH: A|= width ⋅ height; = 5 ⋅ 4; = 20.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB},] we have
[MATH: A_{1}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 1 ⋅ 4; = 2.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC},] we have
[MATH: A_{2}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 4 ⋅ 3; = 6.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC},] we have
[MATH: A_{3}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 5 ⋅ 1; = 2.5.]

Therefore, the area of [MATH: \triangle ABC] is

[MATH: A_{\triangle} = 20 - 2 - 6 - 2.5 = 9.5]

square units.
